 GST New Rules: Major Relief on Notices, Penalties and Appeals
 Ishwarya Keerthi B 
 Ishwarya Keerthi B 
 Author 
 Follow 
 View profile 
 Last updated: 27 October 2026 
 Save 
 Share 
 Join Us 
 Follow Us

 Introduction
 The GST dispute resolution system in India may become more taxpayer-friendly following the recommendations made at the 57th GST Council meeting on 8 October 2026. The Council recommended several measures aimed at reducing unnecessary litigation, improving the quality of tax notices, rationalising penalties and making appeals more accessible to businesses.
 These proposals address important concerns faced by taxpayers, including notices involving small tax amounts, high financial burdens during appeals and inconsistencies in adjudication proceedings. The reforms are intended to encourage voluntary compliance while maintaining appropriate action against genuine tax violations. However, the proposed changes should not be treated as effective law until the required amendments, notifications or circulars are issued.
 GST Notices Below ₹10,000: Proposed Minimum Threshold
 One of the significant recommendations is to introduce a minimum threshold of ₹10,000 for issuing GST show-cause notices. The proposed threshold would consider the combined amount of CGST, SGST, IGST and cess. Under this recommendation, show-cause notices would not be issued where the tax amount involved is less than ₹10,000.
 The Council has also recommended a provision for dealing with notices and appeals involving amounts below ₹10,000 that are pending when the threshold provision comes into force. Such matters would be decided as if the threshold had applied when the notice was originally issued.
 Example
 Suppose a taxpayer has a disputed GST amount of ₹8,000. If the recommended threshold becomes effective in the proposed form, a new show-cause notice would not be issued for that amount. However, taxpayers should not assume that all existing notices are automatically cancelled. The treatment of pending matters will depend on the final statutory provision and its commencement.
 Why is this change important?
 It could reduce litigation involving small tax amounts.
 It may help tax authorities focus on more significant disputes.
 It could reduce the cost of responding to minor tax demands.
 It may improve the efficiency of GST adjudication.
 Reduction in the General GST Penalty from ₹25,000 to ₹10,000
 The GST Council has recommended reducing the maximum general penalty under Section 125 of the CGST Act, 2017, from ₹25,000 to ₹10,000. Section 125 deals with general penalties for contraventions for which a separate penalty is not specifically provided under the relevant provisions.
 If implemented as recommended, this reduction could provide relief to taxpayers facing general penalty proceedings. The proposal concerns the maximum general penalty under Section 125. It should not be interpreted as a universal cap of ₹10,000 on every GST penalty, tax demand or interest liability. Specific penalty provisions may operate differently. Taxpayers should identify the legal provision cited in a notice before determining potential penalty exposure.
 Reduced Penalty in Certain Non-Fraud Cases
 The Council has recommended a reduced penalty of 5% in specified non-fraud cases where the taxpayer pays the applicable tax and interest within the prescribed period after the adjudication order. The recommended payment periods are:
 Provision 
 Proposed payment period 
 Section 73 
 Within 30 days of the adjudication order 
 Section 74A 
 Within 60 days of the adjudication order 
 The recommendation also includes removing the minimum penalty of ₹10,000 in non-fraud cases. These proposals could reduce the financial burden on taxpayers who settle eligible disputes promptly.
 Example
 Suppose an eligible non-fraud case involves a tax amount of ₹2,00,000, along with applicable interest. A 5% penalty calculated on the tax amount would be ₹10,000. If the final provision adopts this calculation and the taxpayer satisfies all prescribed conditions, the reduced penalty mechanism may apply. The actual amount payable must be determined under the final legal provisions, including the applicable penalty base and payment conditions.
 The proposed relief is conditional. Businesses should check the section under which the demand has been raised, the nature of the alleged default, the date of the adjudication order and the statutory payment deadline before relying on the reduced penalty.
 Voluntary Payment of Tax, Interest and Penalty
 The GST Council has recommended a provision to deem the penalty amount as a charge where the taxpayer voluntarily pays the full tax amount, along with interest and penalty, within the specified time limit. The objective is to provide a clearer legal framework for qualifying voluntary payments and settlement of eligible liabilities.
 Taxpayers receiving a notice should carefully evaluate whether voluntary payment is appropriate in their circumstances. They should also ensure that payments are made under the correct statutory provision and within the applicable deadline. Voluntary payment should not be confused with an automatic waiver of tax or interest.
 Maximum Pre-Deposit Limit for Appeals Involving Only Penalty
 Appeal proceedings can impose a substantial financial burden because taxpayers may be required to deposit a prescribed portion of the disputed amount before their appeals are admitted. The GST Council has recommended amendments to Sections 107(6) and 112(8) of the CGST Act to establish an upper limit of ₹40 crore on the pre-deposit payable for appeals involving only a penalty and no demand of tax.
 ₹20 crore under CGST.
 ₹20 crore under SGST/UTGST.
 The recommendation relates to pre-deposits before the Appellate Authority or the Appellate Tribunal, respectively, in cases where the order involves only a penalty and no tax demand.
 How could this help taxpayers?
 A statutory ceiling on the required pre-deposit could limit the amount that must be deposited to access the appellate process, subject to the final rules. This could make it easier for eligible taxpayers to challenge penalty orders without having to arrange an unlimited proportionate deposit. The proposed ₹40 crore limit is a ceiling on the specified pre-deposit, not a cap on the underlying penalty or a guarantee that an appeal will succeed.

 Clearer Guidelines for GST Notices and Adjudication Orders
 The Council has recommended issuing comprehensive guidelines for tax officers to improve the process of issuing demand notices, adjudication orders and appeal orders. The proposed guidelines would address several areas.
 Quality of notices and orders
 Notices and orders should contain appropriate information and clearly explain the issues under consideration.
 Timely issuance
 The guidelines are intended to promote timely issuance of notices and orders, improving certainty for taxpayers.
 Proper use of fraud-related allegations
 The Council has recommended that allegations involving fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts should be invoked on the merits of each individual case. The legal treatment of a dispute can depend on whether the matter involves a genuine fraud-related allegation or a non-fraud situation.
 Compliance with natural justice
 The proposed guidelines would emphasise principles of natural justice, including the conduct of personal hearings. Taxpayers should have the opportunity to present their explanations and supporting evidence in accordance with the applicable procedure.
 These measures aim to promote more consistent, transparent and legally sound adjudication.
 How Will the Proposed GST Dispute Reforms Benefit Businesses?
 Lower litigation costs: The proposed minimum notice threshold could reduce proceedings involving very small tax amounts.
 Reduced penalty exposure: Eligible non-fraud cases may benefit from the proposed 5% penalty mechanism and removal of the minimum penalty requirement.
 Improved access to appeals: A ceiling on the specified penalty-only appeal pre-deposit could reduce financial barriers to challenging orders.
 Better-quality proceedings: Clearer guidelines may help improve the quality of notices, adjudication orders and appeal orders.
 Greater procedural fairness: Emphasis on natural justice and personal hearings may help taxpayers present their cases more effectively.
 More predictable compliance: Clearer procedures and payment timelines could help businesses make informed decisions when responding to tax disputes.
 The extent of these benefits will depend on the final legal framework and how the measures are implemented.
 What Should Taxpayers Do When They Receive a GST Notice?
 Read the notice carefully and identify the relevant legal provision.
 Verify the tax amount, interest, penalty and period involved.
 Reconcile the notice with GST returns, invoices, ledgers and payment records.
 Check whether the matter involves a fraud-related allegation or a non-fraud dispute.
 Review the applicable response deadline and hearing requirements.
 Evaluate whether a reply, voluntary payment or appeal is appropriate.
 Maintain proof of payments, submissions and acknowledgements.
 Consult a qualified tax professional or legal adviser where the matter involves substantial amounts or complex legal issues.
 The recommended ₹10,000 threshold and penalty relief mechanisms should be applied only after confirming that the relevant provisions have come into force and cover the particular case.
 Are the Proposed GST Penalty and Appeal Changes Already Effective?
 The recommendations were announced in the press release following the 57th GST Council meeting held on 8 October 2026. A Council recommendation does not, by itself, establish that every proposed amendment is already legally effective. The press release expressly states that the recommendations will be given effect through the relevant circulars, notifications or legislative amendments. Taxpayers should therefore check the applicable official notifications and amendments before relying on the proposed concessions.
 Also Read - GST Late Fee Waiver: Relief for Small Taxpayers 
 Conclusion
 The GST Council’s proposed dispute resolution reforms could bring meaningful changes to how smaller tax disputes, penalties and appeals are handled in India. The recommended ₹10,000 threshold for show-cause notices, reduced penalties in eligible non-fraud cases, lower maximum general penalties and a ceiling on specified penalty-only appeal pre-deposits are intended to reduce avoidable litigation and financial pressure on taxpayers. Businesses should distinguish between announced recommendations and legally effective amendments. Until the relevant provisions are notified and brought into force, taxpayers should continue to follow the existing applicable law and seek professional advice when responding to GST disputes.
 FAQs
 1. What is the proposed minimum GST notice threshold? 
 The GST Council has recommended a minimum threshold of ₹10,000, combining CGST, SGST, IGST and cess. Under the proposal, show-cause notices would not be issued where the tax amount involved is below this threshold.
 2. Will existing GST notices below ₹10,000 be cancelled? 
 Not automatically. The Council has recommended a statutory provision for pending notices and appeals involving amounts below ₹10,000. Their treatment will depend on the final provision and its commencement.
 3. Has the maximum general GST penalty been reduced to ₹10,000? 
 The Council has recommended reducing the maximum general penalty under Section 125 of the CGST Act from ₹25,000 to ₹10,000. The change must be implemented through the required legal process.
 4. What is the proposed 5% GST penalty rule? 
 The Council has recommended a 5% penalty in specified non-fraud cases where tax and interest are paid within 30 days under Section 73 or 60 days under Section 74A of the adjudication order, subject to the final statutory conditions.
 5. Is the ₹40 crore appeal pre-deposit limit applicable to every GST appeal? 
 No. The recommendation specifically concerns appeals involving only a penalty and no demand of tax, before the Appellate Authority or the Appellate Tribunal, respectively.
 6. What is the purpose of the proposed GST dispute resolution reforms? 
 The objective is to reduce unnecessary litigation, rationalise penalties, improve notice and order quality, and make the appeal process more accessible for taxpayers.
 7. Will fraud-related GST cases receive the same penalty relief? 
 The proposed reduced penalty mechanism is directed at specified non-fraud cases. The applicable treatment depends on the nature of the allegation and the final statutory provisions.
 8. Should taxpayers ignore notices involving small amounts? 
 No. Taxpayers should continue to respond within applicable deadlines unless the relevant law provides otherwise. They should verify whether any new threshold provision has become effective and applies to their case.
